item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Kid-friendly Hikes Under 3 Miles

One Oakland redwood trail runs a flat, paved mile and a half that a stroller finishes, rated 4.7 stars by the people who actually walked it. Most East Bay parents keep circling the same three crowded parks. Eight East Bay kid hikes under three miles, each with the real mileage and climb.

Stream Trail to Trail's End

Canyon Meadow staging, 7867 Redwood Rd, Oakland, in Redwood Regional Park. 1.7 miles, 91 feet of gain, paved and stroller-friendly, 4.7 stars. The one even a four-year-old finishes. @ebrpd

Sequoia Bayview and Big Trees Loop

Joaquin Miller Park, 3540 Sanborn Dr, Oakland. 2 miles, 219 feet of gain, easy, 4.7 stars. A coast-redwood loop with a bay view.

Overlook and Round Top Loop

Sibley Volcanic Preserve, 6800 Skyline Blvd, Oakland. 1.7 miles, 246 feet of gain, 4.6 stars. A loop around the Bay Area's own extinct volcano.

Lower and Upper Huckleberry Loop

Huckleberry Botanic Preserve, Skyline Blvd, Oakland. 2.3 miles, 367 feet of gain, 4.7 stars. A rare-plant preserve big on birdsong, no dogs on this one.

East West and Upper Jordan Fire Trail

Claremont Canyon Regional Preserve, Claremont Ave, Berkeley. 2.2 miles, 620 feet of gain, 4.6 stars. A short climb that pays off with the full bay and bridge.

Grizzly Peak, Tower, and Golf Course Loop

Tilden Regional Park, Grizzly Peak Blvd, Berkeley. 2.6 miles, 442 feet of gain, 4.5 stars. Ridge views over the whole East Bay.

French, Tres Sendas, and Stream Loop

Canyon Meadow staging, 7867 Redwood Rd, Oakland, in Redwood Regional Park. 2.5 miles, 456 feet of gain, 4.8 stars. The highest-rated of the set, deep in the redwoods.

Sunset, Sequoia Bay View, and Chaparral Loop

Joaquin Miller Park, 3540 Sanborn Dr, Oakland. 2.8 miles, 416 feet of gain, 4.6 stars. Save it for a west-facing sunset finish.

Eight under three miles: the paved Stream Trail, Sequoia Bayview, Round Top, Huckleberry, Claremont Canyon, Grizzly Peak, the French loop, and the Sunset ridge. Which one gets the first Saturday?

item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Summit Hikes, Easy to Hard

The pole at the top of Mission Peak is the most photographed spot in the East Bay, and you earn it with 2,145 feet of climbing. But not every East Bay summit makes you suffer, one is a two mile volcano loop. Nine summit hikes, easy to hard, with the grade and route on each.

Mission Peak Loop

Stanford Ave staging, Fremont, in Mission Peak Regional Preserve. 6.1 miles, 2,145 feet of gain, hard, loop, 4.7 stars. The pole at the summit selfie hike. @ebrpd

Mount Diablo via Summit Trail

Mount Diablo State Park, Walnut Creek. 7.4 miles, 2,152 feet of gain, hard, out and back, 4.7 stars. The highest point for miles, the Sierra crest on a clear day. @castateparks

Panoramic Hill, Chaparral Peak and Strawberry Canyon Loop

Claremont Canyon Regional Preserve, Berkeley. 6.1 miles, 1,505 feet, hard, loop, 4.7 stars. Straight up the Berkeley hills to the full bay.

Wildcat Creek, San Pablo Ridge and Belgum Loop

Wildcat Canyon Regional Park, Richmond. 5.7 miles, 1,305 feet, moderate, loop, 4.6 stars. A ridgeline with bay to Diablo views the whole way.

Springhill, Lafayette Ridge and Briones Crest Loop

Briones Regional Park, Lafayette. 4.2 miles, 1,033 feet, moderate, loop, 4.6 stars. Rolling ranch ridges with Mount Diablo on the horizon.

Dunn, Stream and Graham Loop

Redwood Regional Park, Oakland. 7.5 miles, 1,459 feet, hard, loop, 4.7 stars. The big climb inside the redwoods.

High Ridge Loop

Dry Creek Pioneer Regional Park, Union City. 5.8 miles, 1,227 feet, hard, loop, 4.7 stars. A quieter climb over the south county hills.

Round Top

Sibley Volcanic Preserve, 6800 Skyline Blvd, Oakland. 1.7 miles, 246 feet, easy, loop, 4.6 stars. A volcano summit you reach in two miles, the accessible peak.

Mount Wanda

John Muir NHS, Alhambra Ave, Martinez. 2.4 miles, 544 feet, moderate, out and back, 4.6 stars. Named for John Muir's daughter, oak grassland up to the view.

Nine summits, easy to hard: Mission Peak, Diablo, Panoramic Hill, San Pablo Ridge, Briones Crest, the Redwood Dunn loop, High Ridge, Round Top, and Mount Wanda. Which one is yours?

item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Lakeside Trails

Lake Chabot hides an 8.9-mile shoreline loop that most East Bay walkers never take past the first cove. When the hills go gold and hot in summer, the water trails stay cool. Six East Bay lakeside trails.

Lake Chabot Loop

Lake Chabot Regional Park, Castro Valley. 8.9 miles, 770 feet of gain, 4.8 stars. The full shoreline loop, part paved, with boat rentals at the marina. @ebrpd

Lafayette Reservoir Rim Trail

Lafayette Reservoir Recreation Area, Lafayette. 5 miles, 938 feet of gain, 4.7 stars. A rim loop above the water, with a flat paved lakeside path below.

Lake Anza loop

Tilden Regional Park, Berkeley. About 1.4 miles around the swim lake, sandy beach and summer lifeguards. The one you can actually swim after.

Rocky Ridge and Kings Canyon Loop

EBMUD Lands, Moraga, above Upper San Leandro Reservoir. 6.7 miles, 928 feet of gain, 4.6 stars. Reservoir views the whole ridge, an EBMUD trail permit required.

Jordan Pond via High Ridge

Dry Creek Pioneer Regional Park, Union City. 3.3 miles, 413 feet of gain, 4.7 stars. A pond-and-ridge loop in the south-county hills.

Wildcat Creek Trail to Jewel Lake

Tilden Nature Area, Berkeley. A 1.7-mile flat boardwalk to a little lake, heavy on birds, easy for strollers.

Six for the water: Lake Chabot, Lafayette Reservoir, Lake Anza, Rocky Ridge, Jordan Pond, and Jewel Lake. Which lake gets your summer?

Bay Area Mountain-bike Routes

Tilden alone strings together a 4.3-mile Seaview loop with 994 feet of climb and a straight-shot ridge view, no shuttle and no bridge toll. The East Bay hills are a fire-road playground most riders drive right past. Six East Bay mountain-bike routes.

Seaview and Big Springs Loop

Tilden Regional Park, Berkeley. 4.3 miles, 994 feet of gain, moderate, 4.7 stars. Ridge-top fire road with a bay view. @ebrpd

Wildcat Gorge, Meadows Canyon and Curran Loop

Tilden Regional Park, Berkeley. 3.4 miles, 511 feet of gain, 4.7 stars. A creek-and-meadow loop past Jewel Lake.

Round Top, Volcanic and Skyline Loop

Sibley Volcanic Preserve, Oakland. 3.5 miles, 554 feet of gain, 4.6 stars. Around the extinct volcano and its labyrinths.

West Ridge, Graham and Dunn Loop

Roberts Regional Recreation Area, Oakland. 3.1 miles, 505 feet of gain, 4.7 stars. A tidy redwood-edge loop off Skyline.

Dunn, Graham and West Ridge Loop

Redwood Regional Park, Oakland. 4 miles, 587 feet of gain, 4.7 stars. The Redwood fire-road classic.

Sequoia Bayview Trail

Joaquin Miller Park, Oakland. 4.5 miles, 367 feet of gain, easy, 4.7 stars. A smooth, mostly flat bay-view spin.

Six for the ride: Seaview, Wildcat Gorge, Round Top, the Roberts loop, the Redwood Dunn loop, and Sequoia Bayview. Where do you ride?

item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Dog Trails

There is a 2.5-mile redwood loop in Oakland where dogs run off-leash under the tallest trees around, rated 4.8 stars. Most owners circle the same block; the East Bay hills are built for the long sniff. Six East Bay dog trails.

French, Tres Sendas and Stream Loop

Redwood Regional Park, Oakland. 2.5 miles, 456 feet of gain, off-leash, 4.8 stars. Redwood shade the whole way. @ebrpd

Panoramic Hill and Chaparral Peak Loop

Claremont Canyon Regional Preserve, Berkeley. 6.1 miles, 1,505 feet of gain, off-leash, 4.7 stars. A real climb with a bay payoff, for the athletic dog.

Bay Area Ridge and Round Top Loop

Sibley Volcanic Preserve, Oakland. 3.1 miles, 603 feet of gain, 4.6 stars. Open ridge around the old volcano.

High Ridge Loop

Dry Creek Pioneer Regional Park, Union City. 5.8 miles, 1,227 feet of gain, off-leash, 4.7 stars. Wide-open south-county hills, room to roam.

Springhill, Lafayette Ridge and Briones Crest Loop

Briones Regional Park, Lafayette. 4.2 miles, 1,033 feet of gain, off-leash, 4.6 stars. Cattle-country ridges, keep an eye out for the herd.

Sequoia Bayview Trail

Joaquin Miller Park, Oakland. 4.5 miles, 367 feet of gain, 4.7 stars. An easy shaded out-and-back for the older dog.

Six for the dog: the Redwood French loop, Panoramic Hill, Sibley, High Ridge, Briones Crest, and Sequoia Bayview. Where does your dog run?

item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Backpacking and Overnight Trips

The Ohlone Wilderness Regional Trail runs about 28 miles from Mission Peak through Sunol to Del Valle with backcountry camps you reserve ahead, and most East Bay hikers have no idea they can sleep out this close to home. These are the overnight routes hiding in our own hills. Six East Bay backpacking and overnight trips.

Ohlone Wilderness Regional Trail

Mission Peak Staging, Stanford Ave, Fremont, through Sunol to Del Valle, Livermore. About 28 miles point to point, trail camps by reservation, permit required. The Bay Area's classic multi-day walk. @ebrpd

Rose Peak via Sunol

Sunol Regional Wilderness, 1895 Geary Rd, Sunol. 17.9 miles, 3,927 feet of gain, hard, 4.7 stars. The high country of the Ohlone Wilderness, a long day or a first night out.

Little Yosemite and Backpack Road Loop

Sunol Regional Wilderness, 1895 Geary Rd, Sunol. 5.9 miles, 1,230 feet of gain, moderate, 4.7 stars. Past the Little Yosemite gorge to the Sunol backpack area.

Mission Peak via Ohlone Wilderness Trail

Sunol Regional Wilderness, 1895 Geary Rd, Sunol. 10.2 miles, 2,221 feet of gain, hard, 4.6 stars. The quiet back way up Mission Peak from the Sunol side.

Venados Camp via East Shore Trail

Del Valle Regional Park, 7000 Del Valle Rd, Livermore. 2.4 miles, 144 feet of gain, easy, 4.6 stars. A short walk-in to a lakeside camp, the gentle first backpack.

East Shore and Hetch Hetchy Loop

Del Valle Regional Park, 7000 Del Valle Rd, Livermore. 3.7 miles, 436 feet of gain, moderate, 4.7 stars. Lakeshore miles from the Del Valle base camp.

Six for the overnight: the Ohlone Wilderness Trail, Rose Peak, Little Yosemite, the Mission Peak back way, Venados Camp, and the Del Valle lakeshore. Which one gets your first night under the stars?

item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Birding and Wildlife Trails

Lake Merritt became the first official wildlife refuge in the United States in 1870, right in the middle of downtown Oakland. Pelicans, cormorants, and egrets, no drive required. Eight East Bay spots for birds and wildlife.

Rotary Nature Center at Lake Merritt

600 Bellevue Ave, Oakland. On the shore of that 1870 refuge, a flat 3.1 mile loop with pelicans, cormorants, and egrets downtown. @ebrpd

Coyote Hills Bayview and Meadowlark Loop

Coyote Hills Regional Park, 8000 Patterson Ranch Rd, Fremont. 4.9 miles, 282 feet, easy, loop, 4.7 stars. Marsh boardwalk, then low hills over the bay.

Arrowhead Marsh

Martin Luther King Jr Regional Shoreline, Swan Way, Oakland. 3.7 miles, 22 feet, easy, out and back, 4.6 stars. Tidal marsh on San Leandro Bay, big on rails and shorebirds.

Cogswell Marsh Loop

Hayward Regional Shoreline, West Winton Ave, Hayward. 6.1 miles, 36 feet, easy, loop, 4.6 stars. A levee loop through restored salt marsh.

Don Edwards SF Bay National Wildlife Refuge

1 Marshlands Rd, Fremont. The largest urban wildlife refuge in the country, flat salt marsh trails thick with shorebirds.

Vargas Plateau Golden Eagle and Upper Ranch Loop

Vargas Plateau Regional Park, Morrison Canyon Rd, Fremont. 3.9 miles, 518 feet, moderate, loop, 4.7 stars. Open grassland where golden eagles hunt the ridge.

Lake Chabot via East Shore Trail

Lake Chabot Regional Park, 17600 Lake Chabot Rd, Castro Valley. 3.7 miles, 193 feet, easy, out and back, 4.7 stars. A flat stroller friendly shore walk heavy with waterbirds.

Rankin Park to Franklin Ridge Loop

Carquinez Strait Regional Shoreline, Martinez. 4.1 miles, 1,158 feet, moderate, loop, 4.2 stars. A ridge over the strait where raptors ride the thermals.

Eight for the binoculars: Lake Merritt, Coyote Hills, Arrowhead Marsh, Cogswell Marsh, Don Edwards, Vargas Plateau, Lake Chabot, and the Carquinez ridge. Where do you take them?

item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Flat Paved Bay-shore Walks

Point Isabel sits at the Richmond edge of the bay as one of the largest off-leash dog parks in the country, a flat mile and a half of paved shoreline staring straight at the San Francisco skyline. Most people picture hills when they think East Bay trails and skip the water entirely. Six flat, paved bay-shore walks.

Point Isabel Regional Shoreline

Isabel St, Richmond. 1.9 miles, 13 feet of gain, easy, 4.5 stars. Flat bayshore loop, skyline views, and Mudpuppy's dog wash at the gate. @ebrpd

Point Pinole Regional Shoreline

5551 Giant Hwy, Richmond. 3.2 miles, 147 feet of gain, easy, 4.6 stars, paved. Eucalyptus groves out to a bayside fishing pier.

Crown Memorial State Beach, Shoreline Trail

Otis Dr, Alameda. 4.4 miles, 39 feet of gain, easy, 4.5 stars. The East Bay's swim beach, past the Elsie Roemer bird marsh.

Middle Harbor Shoreline Park

2777 Middle Harbor Rd, Oakland. 2.5 miles, 29 feet of gain, easy, 4.5 stars. A tidal lagoon with container ships gliding past at eye level.

Bay Bridge Trail

Judge John Sutter Regional Shoreline, Maritime St, Oakland. 5.6 miles, 242 feet of gain, paved, 4.6 stars. A gentle rise out under the new Bay Bridge span to the vista point.

Albany Waterfront Trail

McLaughlin Eastshore State Park, Buchanan St, Albany. 1.9 miles, 68 feet of gain, easy, 4.6 stars, paved. Bay Trail past the Albany Bulb art and the mudflats.

Six flat and paved: Point Isabel, Point Pinole, Crown Beach, Middle Harbor, the Bay Bridge Trail, and the Albany waterfront. Which shoreline gets your Sunday?

item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Paved Rail-trail Rides

The Iron Horse Regional Trail runs almost 28 paved, car free miles down an old Southern Pacific rail line from Concord to Pleasanton, dead flat the whole way, and most East Bay riders only ever see the half mile nearest their house. Our old rail beds became a whole network you can ride for hours. Seven flat, paved East Bay rides.

Iron Horse Regional Trail

Concord to Pleasanton, on the old Southern Pacific line. 27.7 miles, 295 feet, paved, easy, 4.6 stars. Flat, car free, threaded past BART stations most of the way. @ebrpd

Alameda Creek Regional Trail

Niles Canyon, Fremont, to Coyote Hills and the bay. About 12 paved miles one way, 177 feet, easy, 4.7 stars. A straight flat creekside spin to the shoreline.

Bay Trail, Oakland and Alameda estuary

Jack London Square to the Bay Farm bridge. Flat paved bayfront miles with the skyline across the water.

Lafayette-Moraga Regional Trail

Olympic Blvd, Lafayette, to Moraga, on the old Sacramento Northern line. About 7 miles one way, easy, paved, 4.6 stars. Shaded creekside into downtown Moraga.

Contra Costa Canal Trail

Walnut Creek to Concord along the canal. 13.6 miles, 308 feet, easy, paved, 4.5 stars. Flat waterside miles linking parks and BART.

Ohlone Greenway

Berkeley to El Cerrito under the BART tracks. 10.7 miles, 246 feet, easy, paved, 4.4 stars. A flat urban rail trail past murals and community gardens.

Nimitz Way

Inspiration Point, Tilden Regional Park, Berkeley. 3.1 miles, 206 feet, easy, paved, 4.7 stars. The one paved ride with a full bay and Briones view.

Seven for two wheels: the Iron Horse, Alameda Creek, the Bay Trail estuary, Lafayette-Moraga, the Contra Costa Canal, the Ohlone Greenway, and Nimitz Way. Which one do you roll first?

item.content:encoded:
Bay Area National Parks Within a Day's Drive

Pinnacles is the only national park in the Bay Area, an ancient volcano split and dragged some 200 miles north by the San Andreas Fault, and it is one of the last places you can watch wild California condors ride the thermals. Most people drive to Yosemite and never notice the park two hours south. Six national parks within a day's drive of the East Bay.

Pinnacles National Park

5000 East Entrance Rd, Paicines. Condor Gulch to High Peaks Loop, 5.4 miles, 1,633 feet of gain, hard, 4.8 stars. Wild condors overhead and the rock spires up close. Go at first light in summer, it bakes. @pinnaclesnps

Point Reyes National Seashore

Bear Valley Trailhead, 1 Bear Valley Rd, Point Reyes Station. Bear Valley Trail to the coast, 9.1 miles, 744 feet of gain, moderate, 4.7 stars. A fern canyon that opens onto the open Pacific. @pointreyesnps

Muir Woods National Monument

1 Muir Woods Rd, Mill Valley. Main Trail, 1.5 miles, 45 feet of gain, easy, 4.8 stars, paved. Old-growth redwoods over 250 feet tall, parking reservation required, book ahead online.

Tennessee Valley Trail

Golden Gate National Recreation Area, Tennessee Valley Rd, Mill Valley. 3.5 miles, 183 feet of gain, easy, 4.7 stars. A flat, stroller-friendly walk out to a hidden pocket beach. @goldengatenps

Mount Wanda

John Muir National Historic Site, 4202 Alhambra Ave, Martinez. 2.4 miles, 544 feet of gain, moderate, 4.6 stars. The oak hills John Muir walked with his daughters, right here in the East Bay. @johnmuirnps

Rosie the Riveter WWII Home Front National Historical Park

1414 Harbour Way South, Richmond. The Bay Trail runs the waterfront past the historic Ford Assembly Building, free visitor center open daily 10 to 5. The national park in our own backyard. @rosietheriveternps

Six within a day's drive: Pinnacles, Point Reyes, Muir Woods, Tennessee Valley, Mount Wanda, and Rosie the Riveter in Richmond. Which national park do you hit first?

item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Shaded Redwood and Creek Hikes for a Hot Day

The redwoods in Redwood Regional Park once grew so tall that ships in the bay used them as a landmark to steer around Blossom Rock, until they were logged in the 1850s. The second-growth grove that came back is the coolest, shadiest ground in the East Bay. Six shaded redwood and creek hikes for a hot day.

Stream, Mill and French Loop

Redwood Regional Park, 7867 Redwood Rd, Oakland. 4.6 miles, 921 feet of gain, moderate, 4.8 stars. Creekside redwood shade the whole way. @ebrpd

Leona Canyon Trail

Leona Canyon Open Space, Canyon Oaks Dr, Oakland. 2.8 miles, 465 feet of gain, easy, 4.4 stars. A cool creek canyon most Oakland hikers walk right past.

Lower and Upper Huckleberry Loop

Huckleberry Botanic Preserve, Skyline Blvd, Oakland. 2.3 miles, 367 feet of gain, moderate, 4.7 stars. A shaded rare-plant preserve, no dogs on this one.

Wildcat Gorge, Meadows and Curran Loop

Tilden Nature Area, Central Park Dr, Berkeley. 3.4 miles, 511 feet of gain, moderate, 4.7 stars. Creek and bay-tree shade to a little lake.

Pioneer Tree Trail

Samuel P. Taylor State Park, 8000 Sir Francis Drake Blvd, Lagunitas. 2.1 miles, 193 feet of gain, easy, 4.7 stars. An old-growth redwood loop in a cool canyon, worth the drive. @castateparks

West Ridge and Graham Loop

Roberts Regional Recreation Area, 10570 Skyline Blvd, Oakland. 3.1 miles, 505 feet of gain, moderate, 4.7 stars. Redwood shade off Skyline, with a swim pool at the base.

Six for the shade: Redwood Regional, Leona Canyon, Huckleberry, Wildcat Gorge, Samuel P. Taylor, and Roberts. Where do you hide when the hills turn gold and hot?

item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Lakes with a Swim Beach

Shadow Cliffs in Pleasanton was a gravel quarry until the 1960s, and now it is a spring fed swim lagoon with a sandy beach and summer lifeguards. The East Bay hides a handful of lakes you can actually swim in when the valley bakes. Seven East Bay lakes with a swim beach.

Shadow Cliffs

2500 Stanley Blvd, Pleasanton. A 1.2 mile shoreline loop, easy, 4.4 stars. Spring fed swim lagoon, sandy beach, summer lifeguards and a water slide. @ebrpd

Del Valle

7000 Del Valle Rd, Livermore. Two swim beaches on a five mile reservoir, lifeguards in summer, with the shoreline trail if you want to walk it off.

Lake Temescal

6500 Broadway, Oakland. A 1 mile shore loop, 4.5 stars. A sandy swim beach right off Highway 24, summer lifeguards, in town.

Lake Anza

Central Park Dr, Tilden Regional Park, Berkeley. A sandy swim beach tucked in the Berkeley hills with seasonal lifeguards. Check that the beach is open before you drive up.

Don Castro

Woodroe Ave, Hayward. A roped off swim lagoon with a 1.5 mile loop around it, 4.1 stars. Shallow and family friendly.

Cull Canyon

18627 Cull Canyon Rd, Castro Valley. A small fenced swim lagoon with a sand beach and seasonal EBRPD lifeguards, the quiet one.

Quarry Lakes

2100 Isherwood Way, Fremont. A swim beach on a Fremont lake with lifeguards in summer, inside a larger recreation area.

Seven to cool off: Shadow Cliffs, Del Valle, Lake Temescal, Lake Anza, Don Castro, Cull Canyon, and Quarry Lakes. Summer algae can close a beach, so call ahead, then which lake gets the towel?

item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Trail-running Loops

Redwood Regional Park hides a shaded single-track called the French Trail, soft dirt under second-growth redwoods that runners loop for the cool and the quiet, 4.6 miles with under a thousand feet of climb. The East Bay hills are laced with runnable loops most people only ever walk. Six East Bay trail-running loops.

Stream, Mill and French Loop

Redwood Regional Park, 7867 Redwood Rd, Oakland. 4.6 miles, 921 feet of gain, moderate, 4.8 stars. The shaded French Trail single-track, soft underfoot. @ebrpd

Seaview Trail

Tilden Regional Park, Berkeley. 6 miles, 1,282 feet of gain, moderate, 4.7 stars. A ridge run with bay-to-Diablo views the whole way.

Rocky Ridge View and Elderberry Loop

item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Wildlife to See Within a Day's Drive (and When)

In 1987 there were 22 California condors left alive on Earth. Pinnacles National Park is one of the places that brought them back, and on a clear morning you can watch a nine-foot wingspan ride the thermals over the High Peaks. The Bay Area is one of the great wildlife corners of California. Six animals to see within a day's drive, and when.

California condors

Pinnacles National Park, Paicines. Look up from the High Peaks or Condor Gulch in the cool morning hours. Year-round, one of the few places on Earth to see a wild condor. @pinnaclesnps

Tule elk

Tomales Point, Point Reyes National Seashore. A free-roaming herd on the northern tip, bugling and clashing antlers in the fall rut from August to October, present year-round. @pointreyesnps

Gray whales

Point Reyes Lighthouse, Point Reyes National Seashore. The migration streams close past the headland from mid-January through April, a prime spot to watch whales from land.

Elephant seals

Chimney Rock, Point Reyes National Seashore. A breeding colony hauls out on the beaches December through March, with pups by January. Winter only, and worth the drive.

Harbor seals and sea lions

Marin Headlands, Golden Gate National Recreation Area. Haul-outs and barking colonies along the coast, with whales offshore in the fall. Year-round. @goldengatenps

Banana slugs

Muir Woods National Monument, Mill Valley. The forest floor's bright yellow icon, out after rain and on cool mornings, while coho salmon spawn in Redwood Creek in winter. Year-round.

Six to see: condors at Pinnacles, tule elk and gray whales at Point Reyes, elephant seals at Chimney Rock, seals in the Marin Headlands, and banana slugs at Muir Woods. Which one first?

item.content:encoded:

Point San Pablo, Richmond. An 1874 Victorian light on an island in the strait, now a five room bed and breakfast reached by the innkeeper's boat. The East Bay's most surprising overnight, book months ahead.

Point Bonita Lighthouse

Marin Headlands, Sausalito. A half mile walk through a hand dug tunnel and across a little suspension bridge to the light on the cliffs, open Sunday and Monday. The Golden Gate framed behind you the whole way.

Point Reyes Lighthouse

Point Reyes National Seashore. Three hundred and eight steps down a wind hammered headland, the best land based gray whale watching in winter. Check that the stairs are open before the drive.

Pescadero. One of the tallest lighthouses on the West Coast at 115 feet, a hostel wrapped around its base and tide pools below. Sunset here is the whole trip.

Oakland. Kayaks, canoes, and pedal boats from the Lake Merritt Boating Center on a tidal lagoon that has been a bird refuge since 1870. Paddle it at golden hour with the necklace of lights coming on.

Castro Valley. The marina at 17936 Lake Chabot Road rents kayaks, pedal boats, and pontoons on a still reservoir ringed by hills. No swimming, but ospreys dive and the coves go quiet fast.

Indian Rock Park

Berkeley. A giant volcanic outcrop rising out of a North Berkeley neighborhood, stone steps to the top and the whole bay at sunset. The city's best free overlook.

Castle Rock

Santa Cruz Mountains. Sandstone tafoni formations pocked like Swiss cheese on a ridge above Saratoga, a favorite of boulderers and kids scrambling the rocks. Cool and forested.

Rock City

Mount Diablo State Park, Clayton. A cluster of sandstone wind caves and honeycombed boulders near the south gate, kids scrambling through the Sentinel Rock tunnels. An easy stop on the drive up Diablo.

Ohlone Wilderness Trail

Sunol to Del Valle. A rugged twenty eight mile point to point over Rose Peak, backcountry camps you reserve, and a permit that comes with a gate key. The East Bay's real backpacking.

Point Reyes Coast Camps

Henry Coe State Park

Morgan Hill. The largest state park in Northern California, a vast quiet wilderness of oak ridges and creek pools, wildflowers in spring and total solitude. Bring a map and water.

Big Basin Skyline to the Sea

Saratoga to Santa Cruz. A downhill point to point through the redwoods to the ocean with a camp at Waterman Gap, the classic Bay Area thru hike, reopening as the park recovers. Check current status.

Sunol Backpack Area

Sunol Regional Wilderness. A gentle first backpack, a few miles in to a hillside camp with oak shade and a creek, close enough to bail if the kids melt down. The training trip.

Del Valle Shoreline

Berkeley. A short paved all access nature trail near the Little Farm with braille and low signage, built for every visitor. Pair it with feeding the farm animals.

Full moon hike, Tilden Park

Night programs, Sunol Wilderness

Coyote Hills after dark

Fremont. Full moon marsh walks over the boardwalks with the tide and the frogs, flat and family friendly. One of the gentler night hikes to try first.

Del Valle Regional Park

Livermore. Summer evening naturalist programs and star parties down by the lake, darker skies away from the city glow and the water mirroring the moon. Check the parks calendar.

Mount Tamalpais astronomy nights

Marin. Evening star programs near Rock Spring and the mountain theater, sunset over the ocean and then the Milky Way. Dress warm, it drops fast.

item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Point Reyes National Seashore Hikes

Point Reyes sits on the far side of the San Andreas fault, a peninsula slowly sliding north on the Pacific plate, laced with 150 miles of trail to the sea. Eight Point Reyes hikes for a day on the edge of the continent.

Bear Valley Trail to the Coast

Point Reyes. 9.1 miles, moderate, out and back, 4.7 stars. The gentle valley walk from the visitor center out to Arch Rock and the ocean bluffs. The signature hike.

Tomales Point

Point Reyes. About 9.5 miles out and back through the tule elk reserve at the peninsula's tip, ocean on both sides and bulls bugling in fall. Bring binoculars.

Alamere Falls via Palomarin

Point Reyes. About 13 miles round trip past two lakes to a rare tidefall pouring onto the beach. Time it with low tide and give it the day.

Mount Wittenberg via Sky Trail

Point Reyes. 5.2 miles, moderate, 4.7 stars. A climb to the peninsula's high point through fir forest with ocean views at the top. The lung stretcher.

Sculptured Beach via the Coast Trail

Point Reyes. 6.5 miles, moderate, 4.6 stars. Down to a wave carved beach of sandstone shelves and tide pools at low tide. Check the tide chart.

Chimney Rock

Point Reyes. A short bluff walk out a narrow point, wildflowers in spring, elephant seals below in winter, gray whales offshore. The quick dramatic one.

Estero Trail

Point Reyes. A rolling path along a tidal estuary to Drakes Estero, herons and harbor seals and almost no crowds. The quiet birding walk.

Earthquake Trail

Bear Valley. A flat half mile paved loop straddling the San Andreas fault, a fence offset twenty feet by the 1906 quake. History underfoot, stroller friendly.

Eight on the seashore: Bear Valley, Tomales Point, Alamere Falls, Mount Wittenberg, Sculptured Beach, Chimney Rock, Estero, and the Earthquake Trail. Which first?

Cataract Falls

Matt Davis to Rock Spring Loop

Mount Tam. 8.8 miles, hard, 4.8 stars. A grassland and forest loop with wide ocean views off the mountain's flank. The all day ramble.

Bon Tempe Lake Loop

Mount Tam Watershed. 4.2 miles, easy, loop, 4.8 stars. A flat, shaded lap around a reservoir with fishing and birds, gentle for families. The easy water walk.

Bootjack and Ben Johnson Loop

Mount Tam. 5.9 miles, moderate, 4.8 stars. A loop dropping into Muir Woods old growth and back up through the fir, redwoods without the reservation crowd. The tree lover's hike.

Mountain Home to East Peak

Mount Tam. 4.1 miles, hard, out and back, 4.7 stars. A steady climb to the summit lookout with the whole bay unrolling below. Earn the top.

Nora Trail to Hogback

Mount Tam. 3.8 miles, moderate, 4.8 stars. A shorter creekside climb to a waterfall and a ridge view, a good half day. The quick one.

East Bay Hidden Staircase Walks

More than 400 hidden public staircases and garden paths lace the Berkeley and Oakland hills, most of them known only to the neighbors who climb them. Eight East Bay secret stairways to walk.

Rose Walk

Berkeley. A landmark double stairway designed by Bernard Maybeck in 1913, curving up through a garden between Euclid and Le Roy. The most beautiful stair in the hills.

Tamalpais Path

Berkeley. Stone steps climbing from Euclid up toward the Rock parks, one of the classic north Berkeley path walks. Steep and leafy.

The Cragmont paths

Berkeley. A tangle of steps like Sterling, Acacia, and Easter Way linking the streets around Cragmont Rock Park, a full loop of stairs and views. Bring a map.

Indian Rock and Mortar Rock steps

Berkeley. Stone stairs carved right into the volcanic outcrops, climbing to a sunset view over the bay. The stairs that end at the top of a rock.

The Oakmore steps

Oakland. A network of concrete stairways stitching the Dimond Canyon and Oakmore hills, hidden between the craftsman homes. The Oakland classic.

Crocker Highlands paths

Oakland. Quiet garden stairways winding through one of Oakland's prettiest old neighborhoods above Lakeshore. The genteel stroll.

Rockridge to Claremont paths

Oakland. Hidden lanes and steps linking the streets above College Avenue up toward the Claremont, a leafy climb. The uphill shortcut.

La Loma and Glendale steps

Berkeley. A steep set of hillside stairs with framed bay views between the switchbacks, part of the north Berkeley path grid. The workout with a view.

Eight secret stairways: Rose Walk, Tamalpais Path, the Cragmont paths, Indian Rock, the Oakmore steps, Crocker Highlands, Rockridge to Claremont, and La Loma. Which climb first?

Donner Canyon and Falls

Mount Diablo SP. 5.5 miles, moderate, 4.7 stars. A shorter route to the same falls through a wildflower canyon, best February to April. The spring classic.

Grand Loop

Mount Diablo SP. 6.4 miles, hard, loop, 4.7 stars. A high loop near the summit past wind carved outcrops and huge views. The greatest hits ring.

Summit Trail

Mount Diablo SP. 7.4 miles, hard, out and back, 4.7 stars. The full climb to the 3,849 foot summit and its stone visitor center. Bag the peak on foot.

Mount Diablo SP. 3.9 miles, moderate, loop, 4.7 stars. A shorter high country loop with big views without the full summit slog. The half day option.

Rock City to the Summit

Mount Diablo SP. 8 miles, hard, 4.7 stars. Start among wind carved sandstone caves kids love to scramble, then climb to the top. Play in the rocks first.

Mitchell Canyon to Eagle Peak

Mount Diablo SP. 8.2 miles, hard, loop, 4.7 stars. A quieter north side climb up a ridge to a sharp peak, wildflowers in spring. The locals' side.

Rock City

Mount Diablo SP. A cluster of sandstone formations and wind caves near the south gate, short scrambles and a gymnasium of rock for families. The easy stop.

item.content:encoded:
Bay Area A Day On Angel Island

Angel Island is the largest island in San Francisco Bay, reached only by ferry, with a summit view that takes in the whole bay and a history as the Ellis Island of the West. Eight ways to spend a day on Angel Island.

Perimeter Road

Angel Island. A five mile paved loop circling the island with a new bay view around every bend, walk it or bike it. The essential lap.

Mount Livermore Summit

Angel Island. A climb up the North Ridge and Sunset trails to the 788 foot top, a full turn of the bay, bridges, and city. The big payoff.

Immigration Station

Angel Island. The preserved Ellis Island of the West where a quarter million people were processed, the barracks poetry carved in the walls a moving museum. Take the tour.

Ayala Cove

Angel Island. The ferry landing with a visitor center, a green lawn, and picnic tables, the easy base for the day. Start and end here.

Camp Reynolds

Angel Island. A Civil War era army post of brick and white clapboard buildings above a west facing beach. Step into the 1860s.

Battery Ledyard and the missile site

Angel Island. Concrete gun batteries and a Cold War Nike missile radar site, the island's layered military past. Poke through the ruins.

Ferry from Tiburon

Angel Island. The short hop from Tiburon or the longer ride from the city, the approach itself a highlight. Sit up top on the way over.

Angel Island beaches

Angel Island. Quiet coves like Quarry and Perles for a picnic with a downtown skyline backdrop. Pack a lunch.

Eight on the island: the Perimeter Road, Mount Livermore, the Immigration Station, Ayala Cove, Camp Reynolds, the batteries, the ferry, and the beaches. Where do you start?

Tilden Park crowns the Berkeley hills with a hand carved 1911 carousel, a working little farm, a steam train, and a swimming lake, all free to wander. Eight ways to spend a day in Tilden.

Central Park Dr. A free farm where kids feed cows, goats, and chickens, bring celery and lettuce to hand out. The toddler favorite.

Central Park Dr. A tucked away swimming lake with a small beach, lifeguards on summer days from late morning to evening. Swim on a hot afternoon.

Jewel Lake

Henry Cowell Redwoods

The Sonoma Coast is where the Russian River pours into the Pacific at Jenner, a wild stretch of bluffs and coves where harbor seals pup on the sand and gray whales pass offshore. Eight Sonoma Coast stops.

Bodega Head

Bodega Bay. A 1.7 mile bluff loop, 4.8 stars, one of the best whale watching perches on the coast in winter. Scan for spouts.

Goat Rock Beach

Jenner. The broad beach at the Russian River mouth where a harbor seal colony hauls out and pups in spring. Keep your distance from the seals.

Kortum Trail

Bodega Bay. A 4 mile bluff path, 4.7 stars, past sea stacks and wildflowers between Shell Beach and Blind Beach. The classic coast walk.

Jenner and the river mouth

Jenner. The tiny town on the hill where the river meets the sea, kayak rentals and a view down the coast. Paddle the estuary.

Salt Point State Park

Jenner. A rugged park of honeycombed tafoni sandstone, tide pools, and a pygmy forest up the hill. Explore the rock formations.

Shell Beach

Bodega Bay. A tide pool cove at the Kortum Trail's south end, rich with anemones and stars at low tide. Time the low tide.

Duncans Landing

Bodega Bay. A dramatic rocky headland and small beach, once a schooner landing, big surf and views. The quick pullout stop.

Fort Ross

Jenner. A restored 1812 Russian fur trading fort on the bluffs, a reconstructed stockade and chapel to walk through. Step into the history.

Oakland. The Stream Trail winds through the regrown coast redwood forest where the famous navigation trees once stood. Walk the valley floor.

Oakland. A hidden creek canyon preserve with a wildflower trail few people know. The local secret.

Pinnacles is the eroded half of a volcano that the San Andreas fault has dragged 200 miles from where it erupted, now California's newest national park and a refuge for condors. Eight Pinnacles hikes and caves.

High Peaks and Condor Gulch Loop

Pinnacles. 5.4 miles, hard, 4.8 stars, through the spires on carved steps and railings, the best chance to see condors. The signature hike.

Bear Gulch Cave and Reservoir

Pinnacles. The Moses Spring loop, 2 miles, 4.8 stars, through a talus cave to a cliff ringed reservoir. Bring a headlamp.

Balconies Cave

Pinnacles. A 2.7 mile loop scrambling through a boulder cave under towering rock walls. The other great cave.

Juniper Canyon to High Peaks

Pinnacles. 4.3 miles, hard, 4.9 stars, a steep climb from the west side into the spires. The quieter way up.

Condor Gulch Overlook

Pinnacles. A 2 mile out and back to a railed overlook facing the High Peaks, a shorter taste of the park. The quick view.

High Peaks and Bear Gulch Loop

Pinnacles. A 7.5 mile grand loop linking the caves, the reservoir, and the spires. The all day circuit.

Old Pinnacles to Balconies

Pinnacles. A gentler 5.4 mile creekside route to the Balconies cave and cliffs. The easier cave approach.

The condors

Pinnacles. Watch for the reintroduced California condors, tagged and soaring on nine foot wings over the High Peaks. Look up at dusk.

Richmond. An island lighthouse turned bed and breakfast, reached by boat. Book the overnight.

Lime Point Lighthouse

Sausalito. A fog station at the very foot of the Golden Gate Bridge. Walk down from the bridge.

Chabot Space and Science Center

10000 Skyline Blvd, Oakland. An Oakland hills center with free Friday night telescope viewing. Look through the big telescope.

Lick Observatory

Mount Hamilton, San Jose. A historic mountaintop observatory above the valley. Drive up for the summer visitor nights.

Morrison Planetarium

55 Music Concourse Dr, San Francisco. The Cal Academy dome, one of the largest all digital planetariums. Catch a full dome show.

Lawrence Hall of Science

1 Centennial Dr, Berkeley. A hilltop science center with a planetarium and a bay view. See a live sky show.

Foothill Observatory

Los Altos Hills. A college observatory with public night viewings. Peer at Saturn's rings.

Fujitsu Planetarium

De Anza College, Cupertino. A South Bay planetarium with public shows. Recline for the star show.

Randall Museum

199 Museum Way, San Francisco. A free hilltop museum with science exhibits and a bay view. Explore the animal room.

Robert Ferguson Observatory

Sugarloaf Ridge, Kenwood. A Sonoma observatory in a dark sky park. Come for a star party.

item.title: Mission Peak and Sunol Hikes
item.description: Eight East Bay hikes around Mission Peak and Sunol, ranked from the lung-buster to the stroll. Fremont and Sunol hold some of the Bay Area's best ridge cli
item.content:encoded:
Mission Peak and Sunol Hikes

Eight East Bay hikes around Mission Peak and Sunol, ranked from the lung-buster to the stroll. Fremont and Sunol hold some of the Bay Area's best ridge climbs, and locals know which trailhead to pick. Here's your map to the good stuff.

Mission Peak via Stanford Avenue

Mission Peak Regional Preserve, Fremont. The classic gut-check: a 3-plus-mile climb to the summit that eats about five hours round trip once you count the photo line at the pole. Only 43 spots in the lot, so it fills before the coffee kicks in. Come on a weekday and you dodge the resident parking rules. @ebrpd

Hidden Valley Trail

Mission Peak Regional Preserve, Fremont. This is the steep line the district itself files under its challenging hikes, the one that turns your calves into a talking point. Open grassland the whole way up and almost no shade, so save it for a cool morning. The reward is that same summit ridge.

Mission Peak via Ohlone College

Mission Peak Regional Preserve, Fremont. The Peak Trail here is the gentler grade and part of the Bay Area Ridge Trail, that 550-plus-mile ring around the bay. Over 900 parking spaces and a four dollar machine, so the walkable payoff is you find a spot without circling. Passes a horse corral and shaded woodland the Stanford side never sees. @ebrpd

Ohlone Wilderness Trail

Mission Peak to Sunol, Alameda County. Twenty-nine miles of ridgeline linking Mission Peak to Del Valle, and here's the 2026 news: as of January 1 you no longer need the old Ohlone permit to hike it. Overnight camping still wants a reservation. Do an out-and-back chunk from the Stanford staging area and turn around when your legs vote.

Flag Hill Trail

Sunol Wilderness Regional Preserve, Sunol. A short 1.26 miles one way, but the switchbacks are steep enough to make it honest work before the view opens on Calaveras Reservoir and the Alameda Creek watershed. Look down and you're standing on fossil-bearing sandstone, an old seabed parked in the hills. @ebrpd

Canyon View Trail

Sunol Wilderness Regional Preserve, Sunol. A gentle 1.39-mile rise through Jacob's Valley that hands you off to Little Yosemite, the scenic long way, not the grind. Weathered serpentine and sandstone outcrops line it, and the oak woodland keeps it civilized. Good pick when the peak crowd wants a mellower local loop.

Little Yosemite (Alameda Creek Overlook)

Sunol Wilderness Regional Preserve, Sunol. A scenic gorge on Alameda Creek about two miles upstream from the Visitor Center, all boulders and green pools. The district officially renamed it Alameda Creek Overlook, and no, you can't swim: endangered species live in that water. Pack a lunch and a flat rock to sit on.

Maguire Peaks Loop

Sunol Wilderness Regional Preserve, Sunol. A 3.9-mile loop off the beaten Sunol track, with views of San Antonio Reservoir and Mt. Diablo and plants that grow rare everywhere else in the park. Park on Welch Creek Road and note the weekend permit fee at the kiosk. Quiet is the whole point out here. @ebrpd

Eight for the Fremont and Sunol high country: Mission Peak from Stanford, Hidden Valley, Mission Peak from Ohlone, the Ohlone Wilderness Trail, Flag Hill, Canyon View, Little Yosemite and Maguire Peaks. Which East Bay climb gets your next cool Saturday?

item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Briones and Las Trampas Ridge Hikes

Eight East Bay ridge hikes where the Bay Area quietly shows off. Most people gun for Mission Peak and skip the Briones and Las Trampas crests next door, where 1,483-foot Briones Peak opens a 360 on the Delta, Tam, and Diablo. Contra Costa's best-kept ridges, mapped.

Briones Crest Trail

Briones Regional Park, Lafayette. The spine of the park's 6,256 acres, the ridgeline every other trail climbs to meet. Rolling grassland, big oaks, and grazing cattle that hold the right of way, over a view corridor locals blow past on the drive to Tahoe. @ebrpd

Mott Peak Trail

Briones Regional Park, Lafayette. The 1,424-foot high point most people never bother to name, tucked along the crest between the lagoons and Briones Peak. Short pull, big payoff, and on a weekday the summit is usually yours alone. Bring layers, the wind up here does not negotiate. @ebrpd

Briones Peak

Briones Regional Park, Lafayette. At 1,483 feet this is the park's true summit, and the district's own map promises a 360 on the California Delta, Mount Tamalpais, Mount Diablo, and Las Trampas. Clear winter mornings after rain are the move. Naturalist John Muir, who lived in nearby Martinez, hiked these hills, so you are in good company. @ebrpd

Sindicich Lagoons

Briones Regional Park, Lafayette. Twin ponds sitting right up on the crest, reached off the Lagoon Trail, one of the few flat quiet pockets you will find at this elevation. Bring a snack and take in the whole ridge from a spot most hikers skip while chasing the next summit. Golden hour on the water does the work for you. @ebrpd

Las Trampas Rocky Ridge

Las Trampas Wilderness, San Ramon. A paved service road climbs you toward the 2,024-foot summit, then the wind-sculpted stone outcrops take over, colored by lichen the district calls beautiful. Rocky Ridge View Trail bans bikes, so it stays calm. Give the full ridge and the Devil's Hole area a day if you have one. @ebrpd

Las Trampas Ridge Trail

Las Trampas Wilderness, San Ramon. The east ridge across Bollinger Creek, running toward 1,827-foot Las Trampas Peak, with the district crediting views of the Ygnacio, San Ramon, and Amador valleys plus Mount Diablo and the Carquinez Strait. Reach it via Chamise and the Bollinger Creek Loop. Boots recommended, and that is the park talking. @ebrpd

Eugene O'Neill Site and Bollinger Canyon

Las Trampas Wilderness, Danville. Walk in from Danville up the Iron Horse Trail into Las Trampas and finish at the Tao House, the National Park Service parcel of the Eugene O'Neill National Historic Site. The Park Service runs it by reservation, so call ahead before you count on getting in. Oaks and bay laurel the whole climb, and a canyon that feels a county away from I-680. @ebrpd

Elderberry Trail

Las Trampas Wilderness, San Ramon. A quieter hiker line off the Bollinger Creek valley floor, named for the elderberry that fills the chaparral alongside the manzanita and toyon. A low-key way to warm up a Rocky Ridge day before the grade kicks in. Signed and on the district map, unlike the bootleg paths they ask you to skip. @ebrpd

Eight for the Contra Costa skyline: Briones Crest, Mott Peak, Briones Peak, Sindicich Lagoons, Rocky Ridge, Las Trampas Ridge, the O'Neill canyon walk, and Elderberry. Ridge season in the East Bay runs clear and cool right after the first rains. Which crest do you take first?

item.title: Bay Area Coyote Hills and Fremont Shoreline
item.description: Eight stops on the Fremont shoreline, the East Bay corner most people blow past on the way to somewhere else. Coyote Hills is 1,266 acres of marsh and gras
item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Coyote Hills and Fremont Shoreline

Eight stops on the Fremont shoreline, the East Bay corner most people blow past on the way to somewhere else. Coyote Hills is 1,266 acres of marsh and grassland right on the Bay, dedicated back in 1967, and the Alameda Creek Trail and a 30,000-acre wildlife refuge pick up where it leaves off. This is where the map runs out of pavement.

Bayview Trail

Coyote Hills, Fremont. The paved loop runs 3.5 miles around the hills, flat enough for a stroller and high enough to hand you the whole Bay and the peninsula skyline. Locals know it as Sii 'Imnom 'Ommu in Chochenyo, and yes, the wind up top is part of the deal. Go at golden hour and let the fog do the work.

Red Hill Trail

Coyote Hills, Fremont. A short climb to the top of Red Hill, the high point regulars use to catch the breeze and the long view west over the marsh to the water. The Chochenyo name is Pulteewis Saatos. It is the kind of hilltop that explains why the whole neighborhood grew up facing the Bay. Bring a layer, the wind means it.

Marsh Boardwalk

Coyote Hills, Fremont. A raised walkway carries you out over the cattails and open water without soaking a shoe. That's the point of a marsh you can stand in the middle of. Herons and egrets treat the railings like a front porch. Come early on a weekday and you may have the place to yourself.

Chochenyo trail markers

Coyote Hills, Fremont. In 2022 the park unveiled 35 trail markers carrying names in Chochenyo, the language of the Tuibun Ohlone, whose homeland this is. Bayview reads Sii 'Imnom 'Ommu, Red Hill reads Pulteewis Saatos. Read the signs as you walk and the hills stop being scenery and start being a place with a first name.

Tuibun Ohlone shellmound site

Coyote Hills, Fremont. Tucked in the marsh are shellmounds roughly 2,000 years old, left by the Tuibun Ohlone who have lived with this land since long before anyone drew a property line. You reach them on a naturalist-led tour from the visitor center. That's the respectful way in. Book ahead, the walks fill.

Quarry Staging Area

Coyote Hills, Fremont. A staging area with its own picnic tables, barbecue braziers, water, and shade, first come first served, and a quieter place to start than the visitor center lot. It puts you a short walk from the Bayview loop and the marsh. Pack a lunch and claim a table before noon.

Alameda Creek Regional Trail

Fremont. This one runs 12 miles from the Bay to the mouth of Niles Canyon, and it is two trails in one, an equestrian track on the north levee and a paved bike path on the south, bordering Coyote Hills the whole north edge. Ride it end to end and you cross half of Fremont without touching a street.

Don Edwards SF Bay National Wildlife Refuge

1 Marshlands Rd, Fremont. The country's first urban wildlife refuge, set up in 1972, 30,000 acres of open bay and marsh with around 280 kinds of birds passing through. Start on the 0.64-mile Tidelands Trail from the visitor center flagpole, over the footbridge across Newark Slough. Trails run sunrise to sunset, so there is no bad time to wander in.

Eight for a Fremont shoreline day: Bayview loop, Red Hill, the Marsh Boardwalk, the Chochenyo markers, the Ohlone shellmounds, Quarry Staging, Alameda Creek, and the Don Edwards refuge. Bike, boots, or binoculars, which way do you point first?

item.description: Eight ways to spend a morning at Rancho San Antonio, the South Bay preserve everyone in Los Altos and Cupertino treats as their backyard. Over 25 miles of
item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Rancho San Antonio, Los Altos

Eight ways to spend a morning at Rancho San Antonio, the South Bay preserve everyone in Los Altos and Cupertino treats as their backyard. Over 25 miles of trail, a working farm, wild turkeys in the meadow, and a lot that fills by 8am on weekends. Dogs stay home here and water taps are scarce, so pack your own. Here is how to do it right, from easy stroll to real climb.

PG and E Trail

The wide gravel road most people start on, flat and easy the first mile out to the farm, friendly for strollers and little kids. Keep going and it drops the gentle act: the full climb runs 3.7 miles and 1,600 feet up to Black Mountain, fully exposed. Walk the easy mile, or commit to the grind and earn the Bay views up top.

Deer Hollow Farm

A 160-year-old working homestead a flat mile in, with pigs, goats, sheep, chickens and a cow, plus the restored Grant Cabin set up like the late 1800s. Free to walk through and a reliable bribe for anyone you dragged along under four feet tall. Open Tuesday to Sunday 8 to 4, Wednesday until 1, closed Mondays.

Rogue Valley Trail

The shaded creek stretch, cool and green when the exposed hills are baking, poppies and lupine along the edges in spring. This is the section the preserve puts on its own postcards, and you will see why. Take it as the mellow way to loop back, or the smart move on a hot afternoon when the ridge turns into an oven.

Wildcat Loop Trail

A three-mile loop, moderate, that follows the creek into a cool fern-walled canyon, climbs through chaparral to open meadows on the ridge, then drops you back at the farm. On a clear day the meadow hands you Mount Tam to the north and Mount Hamilton to the east. The classic Rancho half-day if you run only one loop.

High Meadow Trail

The climb that trades shade for a payoff, up through grassland to a wide-open ridge meadow where the whole South Bay spreads out below you. Moderate, and you feel the elevation in your legs. String it with Upper Wildcat and PG and E for a roughly 6.5-mile loop. Go on a clear winter morning when the air is scrubbed and the views run for miles.

Upper Wildcat Canyon Trail

Push past where the crowds turn around and this becomes the prettiest, quietest part of the preserve, deep canyon and oak woodland with barely a soul on it. Fold it into the full 7.6-mile Wildcat Canyon Loop, moderate, topping out near 1,050 feet with South Bay vistas. This is where Rancho stops feeling like a city park.

Coyote Trail

Down in the county park, an oak-shaded lower route and the one stretch open to horses, so expect the occasional rider. Easy to moderate, good shade, a calmer alternative when the main drag is packed with strollers and trail runners. Keep your eyes up, coyotes and wild turkeys both work this side of the park.

Chamise Trail to the Windmill Pasture

A 2.1-mile gradual climb to a tranquil hidden meadow at the north end, next to Hidden Villa, where a ranch windmill once stood. Bring a sandwich, this is the picnic spot most Rancho regulars never find. Crews cleared a fuel break along Chamise recently, so parts feel open and sunny now. One of the best quiet corners here.

Eight ways through Rancho San Antonio: PG and E Trail for the easy mile, Deer Hollow Farm for the animals, Rogue Valley for shade, Wildcat Loop for the classic, High Meadow for the views, Upper Wildcat Canyon for quiet, Coyote for the oaks, Chamise for the hidden meadow. Check openspace.org before you leave, come early or midday, bring water, leave the dog home. See you out there.
